items.body:

items.title: Two CVSS 9.0 Linux KSMBD RCE Flaws Disclosed on Public Mailing Lists Before Kernel Fixes
items.body:

Linux servers running KSMBD, the kernel's built-in SMB server, are exposed to two publicly reported remote code execution flaws rated 9.0 by Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative, with no fix yet in the mainline kernel. One of them, ZDI-CAN-33774, can be triggered before any network authentication. The other, ZDI-CAN-33549, requires the SMB Direct transport and an RDMA-capable network

Incus 7.0.0 before 7.0.2 and 7.1.0 before 7.5.0 contains a path traversal vulnerability that allows clients able to create instances to write files on the host. The flaw stems from unvalidated dependent custom volume names in instance backup index.yaml files. Attackers can import a crafted instance backup with ../ sequences in dependent volume names to create root-owned directories with controlled content, leading to full host compromise.

items.title: CVE-2026-96639 — Pillow multi-frame loaders can reuse stale native image storage after mode transitions
items.body:
Vulnérabilité critique CVE-2026-96639 affectant Pillow (pip) (score CVSS 9.8).

Pillow multi-frame loaders can reuse stale native image storage after mode transitions

If frame 0 allocates storage for a narrow mode such as L , and a later frame of the same dimensions switches to a wider mode such as RGB or CMYK , Pillow may decode wider pixels into the stale narrow native buffer. This causes native out-of-bounds writes and process crashes.
items.detail:
Vulnérabilité critique CVE-2026-96639 affectant Pillow (pip) (score CVSS 9.8).

Pillow multi-frame loaders can reuse stale native image storage after mode transitions

If frame 0 allocates storage for a narrow mode such as L , and a later frame of the same dimensions switches to a wider mode such as RGB or CMYK , Pillow may decode wider pixels into the stale narrow native buffer. This causes native out-of-bounds writes and process crashes. In the MPO/JPEG path, I also demonstrated command execution in matching Python/Pillow runtime profiles through Pillow's documented ImageSequence.Iterator + frame.load() path.

The root cause appears to be that ImageFile.load_prepare() only reallocates native storage when _im is None . It does not verify that the retained native ImagingCore storage still matches self.mode and self.size .

Several multi-frame seek() / _open() paths can update self._mode and decoder tiles for a later frame without invalidating _im . The decoder then writes or reads according to the new frame mode while the native storage still belongs to the old frame mode.

PsdImageFile.seek() can switch from grayscale/native L storage to RGB layer decoding while retaining _im . This produces attacker-controlled native out-of-bounds writes and reliable crashes.

A crafted two-frame MPO can make frame 0 allocate L storage, then make frame 1 decode CMYK / RGB data into the retained L storage. The documented ImageSequence.Iterator path reaches this with frame.load() . Verified native memory corruption, crash, over-read behavior, and scoped harmless-marker command execution on Pillow 12.3.0.

While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure.” The activity began on October 17, 2026, and appeared in telemetry from MadPot, AWS’s network of honeypots designed to attract and study malicious activity. The company said the first attempt targeted a honeypot from an IP address linked to a commercial anonymization network. items.title: Managing AI Token Consumption for Operational Resilience
items.body:
Incident de sécurité rapporté par CISA Advisories.

CISA, the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (Cyber Centre), and partners are releasing joint guidance, Managing AI Token Consumption for Operational Resilience , to help organizations understand and manage token usage in support of operations. As organizations adopt third-party super intelligence (SI) services, token-based usage models can affect cost, performance, and access to critical services.
items.detail:
Incident de sécurité rapporté par CISA Advisories.

CISA, the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (Cyber Centre), and partners are releasing joint guidance, Managing AI Token Consumption for Operational Resilience , to help organizations understand and manage token usage in support of operations. As organizations adopt third-party super intelligence (SI) services, token-based usage models can affect cost, performance, and access to critical services. Unmanaged token consumption may contribute to rising and unpredictable costs, reduced service availability, degraded performance, token exhaustion, and denial-of-tokens or denial-of-wallet attacks. The guidance outlines practical steps organizations can take to prioritize token allocation, design efficient workflows, improve user prompting practices, leverage caching and reusable context, optimize data before submission, and monitor token consumption over time. Critical infrastructure owners and operators can use this guidance to identify mission-critical functions that depend on SI, understand service provider and operational dependencies, and plan for reduced SI availability during outages, incidents, or periods of high demand. Cyber defenders can also use the guidance to manage SI-enabled cyber defense workflows while maintaining human oversight, governance, and strong cybersecurity fundamentals.

items.detail:
Incident de sécurité rapporté par Unit 42.

Unit 42 explores modern OAuth threats and actionable steps organizations can take to protect their environments.

As enterprises continue to roll out multi-factor authentication (MFA), attackers have adapted. Rather than only stealing credentials, attackers have shifted to stealing Open Authorization (OAuth) tokens, the keys that govern what applications can do on your behalf. Adversaries are already accelerating these attacks by using dynamic evasion code, phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) templates and LLM-generated brand impersonations.

Because OAuth attacks occur at the authorization layer after user authentication, stolen access and refresh tokens bypass MFA, survive password resets and grant durable access.

While OAuth misuse occurs at a lower volume than traditional phishing attacks, these attacks may carry severe consequences such as:

Defending against these threats can be accomplished using several strategies:

To understand why OAuth has become such a prime target for modern adversaries, it helps to examine the authentication challenges the protocol was originally designed to solve. Looking back at how applications handled identity before OAuth reveals how the threat landscape has evolved from simple password theft to complex token hijacking.

Websites and applications often tie together functionality from other sites. For example, some popular ecommerce and social media platforms allow users to log in through their email accounts.

Participating nations included Angola, Benin, Cameroon, Congo, Côte d'Ivoire, Democratic Republic of Congo, Eswatini, Gabon, Gambia, Ghana, Kenya, Mozambique, Nigeria, Rwanda, Senegal, South Africa, Tanzania, Uganda, United States, Zambia, and Zimbabwe.

Group-IB, which was one of the many private sector partners, said it provided INTERPOL with threat intelligence data on phishing kits, botnets, and other malicious resources hosted in Africa or used to conduct cyber attacks targeting the region.

"Criminals cannot operate without infrastructure. They have to build it, connect it and maintain it, and those activities create opportunities to find them," said Jacomo Piccolini, vice president of Global Data Partnerships at Team Cymru.

"Instead of waiting for an attack and then investigating the damage, we can help expose the networks behind criminal operations and enable defensive actions. Operation Serengeti III demonstrates the real-world impact of putting that intelligence in the hands of law enforcement."

items.title: Encryption isn’t enough to protect data wherever it goes
items.body:
Incident de sécurité rapporté par CyberScoop.

Cybersecurity policy has long treated data protection as a systems problem: encrypt the database, secure the network, restrict access, monitor activity, and keep attackers out. All of that still matters. But those defenses have a major blind spot. Once inside the wall the data itself is at risk. Every time data is used, copied, or moved, the risk that a malicious actor will steal and expose the data significantly increases.
items.detail:
Incident de sécurité rapporté par CyberScoop.

Cybersecurity policy has long treated data protection as a systems problem: encrypt the database, secure the network, restrict access, monitor activity, and keep attackers out. All of that still matters. But those defenses have a major blind spot. Once inside the wall the data itself is at risk. Every time data is used, copied, or moved, the risk that a malicious actor will steal and expose the data significantly increases. Policymakers need to consider a tested method that reduces the value of sensitive information if it compromised. Hospitals, banks, defense contractors and government agencies cannot operate on permanently unreadable data. They need to process records, share information, analyze intelligence and prepare data for artificial intelligence models. The reality is data moves. It travels through cloud platforms, vendors, backups, analytics tools, payment processors, software services, AI pipelines, and partner systems. Every handoff creates another place where information can be copied, cached, logged, and indexed, and another place where it can be mishandled or stolen. This is the gap encryption does not close. Encryption protects data when it is stored or traveling, only partially protects it when it is transmitted, and does not protect data at all when it is processed. Once an authorized system decrypts information so someone can use it, the data becomes readable

items.detail:
Incident de sécurité rapporté par The Record.

Late Wednesday night the Toronto chapter of Crime Stoppers broke ranks with the national association, revealing a timeline showing what it knew and when along with an announcement that it will pause operations.

A Toronto crime prevention program that long promised witnesses a safe space to anonymously report tips froze its operations late Wednesday night, hours after a Canadian news outlet reported that more than 1.5 million tips from Crime Stoppers chapters across the country were exposed in a data breach.

Crime Stoppers urges people not to provide their names when submitting information, but reporters at Canada’s CBC broadcaster were able to reach more than a dozen tipsters by reviewing the hacked data made available to them in March by Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets).

About half of the 1.5 million leaked tips CBC studied — some dating back 25 years — contained personal information, the outlet reported.

While Canadian Crime Stoppers Association and individual chapters, including Toronto’s, had confirmed the breach in the days after the hack, they offered no detail about what was exposed, blaming the lack of information on vendor Navigate360 and its subsidiary, P3 Global Intel.

But late Wednesday night the Toronto chapter broke ranks with the national association, revealing a timeline showing what it knew and when along with an announcement that it will pause operations.

“Since 1984, people in Toronto have come to Toronto Crime Stoppers because we promised they could stay anonymous,” Sean Sportun, chair of Toronto Crime Stoppers, said in a statement . “This week’s reporting shows that for some of them, that promise was broken. We are deeply sorry.”

items.detail:
Incident de sécurité rapporté par The Record.

The issue was publicized by cybersecurity researcher Scott Helme, who published a blog saying that instead of a random 384-bit number, one of the company's private keys was just the number four.

One of the only Indian root certificate authorities trusted by major web browsers said it is withdrawing from the global certificate business after facing significant backlash over a security incident this week.

The company, eMudhra, said it was voluntarily withdrawing from the global SSL/TLS certificate business after the private keys of eight of its intermediate certificates were found to be weak, prompting browsers like Firefox , Apple and Chrome to block the certificates.

According to Google, Mozilla and several other companies, the keys could allow attackers to issue fraudulent HTTPS certificates for websites they do not control. An attacker who could intercept a user’s connection could use those certificates to impersonate websites and potentially read or modify traffic.

Cloudflare explained that the certificates were widely trusted by their own system as well as browsers and operating systems. Because of the weak keys, any attacker could create a forged certificate for any domain and use it to impersonate servers to intercept or modify traffic.

The issue was publicized by cybersecurity researcher Scott Helme, who published a blog saying that instead of a random 384-bit number, one of the private keys was just the number four. Others were simply 56 and 115.

eMudhra said this week that the certificates were created during a ceremony in April 2025 and the ”problem was a flaw in one step of the ceremony procedure.” The issue went undetected for 18 months and survived two independent audits before a researcher reverse engine

items.detail:
Incident de sécurité rapporté par Cyberattaque.org.

Un incident de sécurité majeur touche Railway, la plateforme cloud utilisée par des développeurs pour déployer leurs applications. Le 21 octobre 2026,

cyberactu Mis à jour le 22 octobre 2026 à 6h09 Railway : une cyberattaque menace les accès sensibles de ses clients Un incident de sécurité majeur touche Railway, la plateforme cloud utilisée par des développeurs pour déployer leurs applications. Le 21 octobre 2026, l’entreprise a détecté une activité anormale sur les systèmes chargés de stocker les variables d’environnement de ses clients . Railway reconnaît qu’un tiers non autorisé pourrait avoir accédé à des variables chiffrées et, pour certaines d’entre elles, obtenu leur contenu en clair .

Le problème dépasse largement la fuite de simples paramètres techniques. Les variables d’environnement servent précisément à conserver les secrets d’une application : clés API OpenAI ou Anthropic, mots de passe de bases de données, identifiants AWS ou Google Cloud, clés Stripe, accès aux registres privés ou tokens GitHub . Railway recommande donc à tous ses utilisateurs de les considérer comme potentiellement compromis et de les remplacer immédiatement.

Railway explique que l’activité suspecte concernait directement les systèmes stockant les variables d’environnement de ses clients. L’enquête indique qu’un attaquant a pu consulter des données chiffrées et déchiffrer au moins une partie des valeurs .

Ce point est particulièrement important. Le chiffrement au repos protège normalement un secret en cas de simple copie du stockage, mais une plateforme cloud doit forcément être capable de déchiffrer ces valeurs lorsqu’elle démarre une application ou construit un conteneur . Une compromission suffisamment profonde du système chargé

Nobody reviewed its access. Nobody owns it. If an employee had that much reach with that little oversight, you would call it an insider risk. So why do we still call the agent a productivity tool?

items.title: Bureautique de l’État : la Cour des comptes plaide pour le logiciel libre
items.body:
Signal de veille — Silicon.fr.

Après une critique circonstanciée de la Dinum en 2024 , la Cour des comptes revient sur le sujet de la numérisation des services de l’Etat avec un nouveau rapport intitulé » Les outils bureautiques et collaboratifs au sein de l’Etat ».
items.detail:
Signal de veille — Silicon.fr.

Après une critique circonstanciée de la Dinum en 2024 , la Cour des comptes revient sur le sujet de la numérisation des services de l’Etat avec un nouveau rapport intitulé » Les outils bureautiques et collaboratifs au sein de l’Etat ». L’enquête, déclenchée via la plateforme de participation citoyenne de la juridiction financière, porte sur les administrations centrales et les services déconcentrés des onze ministères, soit environ 861 000 postes informatiques. Quatre d’entre eux en concentrent l’essentiel : l’Intérieur, les Armées, l’Économie et les Finances, et la Justice. Le champ d’étude exclut les collectivités locales, les hôpitaux, les organismes de sécurité sociale et les opérateurs de l’État. Les 850 000 enseignants ne disposent pas d’ordinateurs gérés par l’administration : seuls 30 000 postes administratifs sont comptabilisés pour l’Éducation nationale. Une mosaïque héritée de l’autonomie des ministères Chaque ministère ayant longtemps choisi ses outils, la Cour distingue trois situations. La première, majoritaire, consiste à installer la suite Microsoft Office sur les serveurs ou les postes de l’administration. Cette étape n'est plus obligatoire : Tiny11 Builder dispose désormais d'une vraie application de bureau.

Pour rappel, Tiny11 Builder est le projet open source du développeur NTDEV qui permet de fabriquer une image allégée de Windows 11 à partir d'une ISO officielle de Microsoft.
